question: How do sampling strategies like greedy, top-k, and top-p (nucleus) sampling differ?
directAnswer: These are different ways to pick the next token from the model's probability distribution. Greedy decoding always takes the single highest-probability token, which is deterministic but can be repetitive. Top-k sampling restricts the choice to the k most probable tokens and samples among them. Top-p, or nucleus sampling, instead keeps the smallest set of top tokens whose probabilities sum to a threshold p and samples from that dynamically sized set. Top-p adapts the candidate pool to the model's confidence, which is why it is a popular default over fixed top-k.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
Each strategy defines the candidate set before sampling. Conceptually:
greedy:  pick argmax(probs)
top_k:   keep the k highest, renormalize, sample
top_p:   keep the smallest set summing to >= p, renormalize, sample
Temperature can be applied first to reshape probs in every case.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Pure greedy decoding is deterministic but tends to produce dull, repetitive text and can get stuck in loops, so sampling was introduced for diversity. Top-k limits sampling to plausible tokens to avoid picking absurd low-probability ones, but a fixed k is a poor fit when the distribution is sometimes sharp and sometimes flat. Top-p was created to fix that by sizing the candidate set to the actual shape of the distribution.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: After the model produces logits and (optionally) temperature rescales them, the strategy trims the distribution. Top-k sorts tokens and keeps the top k. Top-p accumulates probability from the most likely token downward until the running sum reaches p, keeping exactly those tokens. The kept probabilities are renormalized to sum to one, and a token is sampled. When the model is confident, top-p keeps few tokens; when it is uncertain, it keeps more, matching the candidate pool to confidence.

whyImportant: Choosing and tuning a sampling strategy directly affects an agent's reliability and an application's tone. Understanding why top-p adapts better than top-k, and when greedy is appropriate, lets you configure generation deliberately. Interviewers ask this to distinguish people who blindly use defaults from those who understand what the decoding parameters actually do.
realWorldExample: A story-generation feature uses top-p around 0.9 so the text stays coherent yet varied, because the nucleus grows when the model is unsure and shrinks when a word is nearly certain, avoiding both robotic repetition and nonsense. A data-extraction agent instead uses greedy or very low temperature, because there is one correct value and any randomness only introduces errors.

nestedTopics.title: Greedy and beam search
nestedTopics.explanation: Greedy decoding always takes the top token, maximizing local probability but often yielding repetitive text. Beam search keeps several candidate sequences and expands the most probable overall, improving quality for tasks like translation, at higher cost and still with a tendency toward generic output.

nestedTopics.title: Top-k sampling
nestedTopics.explanation: Top-k restricts sampling to the k most likely tokens, cutting off the improbable long tail. It prevents bizarre choices but uses a fixed cutoff, which is too restrictive when many tokens are plausible and too permissive when only a couple are, since it ignores the distribution's shape.

nestedTopics.title: Top-p (nucleus) sampling
nestedTopics.explanation: Top-p keeps the smallest set of top tokens whose cumulative probability meets a threshold, so the candidate count varies with the model's confidence. This dynamic behavior generally gives a better balance of coherence and diversity than a fixed k, which is why it is a common default.

followUps.question: Why is top-p often preferred over top-k?
followUps.answer: Because top-p adapts to the shape of the distribution while top-k does not. A fixed k always keeps the same number of candidates regardless of how confident the model is, so when the model is nearly certain, top-k may still admit unlikely tokens, and when the model is genuinely uncertain across many good options, top-k may cut off perfectly reasonable ones. Top-p sizes the candidate set by cumulative probability, so it keeps just a couple of tokens when the model is confident and many when it is not. This confidence-aware behavior tends to give more natural, coherent output across varied contexts, which is why it is a widely used default, though the two can also be combined.

followUps.question: When would you deliberately use greedy decoding in an agent?
followUps.answer: You use greedy decoding, or equivalently temperature zero, when you want the most probable, most consistent output and randomness offers no benefit. Typical cases in an agent are structured output where the JSON must be valid and stable, tool selection where there is a single correct tool and argument set, classification into a fixed label, and extraction of a specific value. In these control-path steps, variability is pure downside: it risks malformed output or wrong tool calls without adding value. You reserve higher-temperature sampling for user-facing creative generation, keeping the agent's decision-making deterministic and debuggable.

question: What are structured outputs and how do you get reliable JSON from an LLM?
directAnswer: Structured output means constraining the model to produce machine-readable output, most often JSON that conforms to a specific schema, so downstream code can parse it without guesswork. You can encourage it through prompting and examples, but the reliable approach uses provider features such as JSON mode or schema-constrained decoding, where the model is forced to emit output matching a supplied JSON Schema. These features work by restricting token generation to only those tokens that keep the output valid against the schema. The result is output you can deserialize directly, which is essential for agents that act on the model's response.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Structured output exists because agents consume the model's response programmatically, and free-form text is fragile to parse: the model might add commentary, use inconsistent keys, or wrap JSON in markdown. Forcing a schema removes that fragility, turning the LLM into a reliable component you can wire into code. It is the foundation of function calling, data extraction, and any pipeline step that feeds the model's output into another system.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Prompt-based approaches simply instruct the model to output JSON and show an example, which helps but can still fail. Constrained decoding is stronger: at each generation step the system masks out any token that would make the output violate the schema or JSON grammar, so only valid continuations are possible. This guarantees the output parses and matches the required structure, at the cost of some flexibility. Providers expose this as JSON mode or a response-format schema parameter.

whyImportant: Reliable structured output is what makes LLMs usable as programmable components rather than chat toys, and it underpins tool calling in agents. Knowing the difference between hoping for JSON via prompting and enforcing it via constrained decoding is a key practical skill. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can build robust integrations instead of fragile string parsing.
realWorldExample: A resume-parsing service asks the model to extract name, email, and a list of skills. Relying on a prompt alone, it occasionally got back a friendly sentence or JSON wrapped in code fences, breaking the parser. Switching to a schema-constrained response format guaranteed a valid object with exactly those fields every time, eliminating a whole class of production errors and letting the code deserialize the output with confidence.

nestedTopics.title: Prompt-based JSON versus enforced schemas
nestedTopics.explanation: Asking for JSON in the prompt and giving an example nudges the model but does not guarantee validity; it may add prose or malform the output. Provider schema enforcement, by contrast, constrains generation so the output must be valid, which is far more reliable for production use.

nestedTopics.title: JSON Schema and function schemas
nestedTopics.explanation: A JSON Schema describes the required fields, types, and structure of the output. The same idea powers function or tool schemas, which describe a tool's parameters so the model can emit a well-formed call. Defining precise schemas, including required fields and enums, improves both correctness and validation.

nestedTopics.title: Constrained decoding
nestedTopics.explanation: Constrained decoding enforces structure by masking out tokens that would break validity at each step, so only schema-conforming continuations are generated. This guarantees parseable output but can slightly limit expressiveness, and it requires the provider or runtime to support grammar-based token filtering.

followUps.question: What can still go wrong even when JSON is syntactically valid?
followUps.answer: Syntactic validity only guarantees the output parses as JSON, not that its contents are correct or complete. The model might return valid JSON with a hallucinated value, an empty string where a real value was expected, a plausible but wrong number, or fields that satisfy the schema types yet are semantically nonsensical. Schema enforcement can require fields and constrain types and enums, which catches structural problems, but it cannot verify factual accuracy. So even with guaranteed-valid JSON, an agent should validate business rules, sanity-check values, and treat the content as untrusted, especially before taking consequential actions based on it.

followUps.question: How does structured output relate to function calling?
followUps.answer: Function calling is essentially structured output applied to tool use. You describe each tool with a schema for its name and parameters, and the model, instead of replying in prose, emits a structured object naming the tool and providing arguments that conform to that schema. The same constrained-generation machinery that produces schema-valid JSON is what produces a well-formed tool call. From the agent's perspective, a function call is just structured output the loop knows how to dispatch: it parses the call, runs the matching function with the arguments, and feeds the result back. So mastering structured output is the prerequisite for reliable tool calling.

question: What is a function or tool schema and why does the model need one?
directAnswer: A function schema is a structured description of a tool the model can call: its name, a natural-language description of what it does, and a typed specification of its parameters, usually expressed as JSON Schema. The model needs this schema because it decides which tool to invoke and with what arguments purely from the descriptions you provide; it has no other knowledge of your functions. A clear name, a precise description, and well-typed parameters with required fields guide the model to choose the right tool and produce valid arguments. The schema is effectively the contract between the model and your code.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Schemas exist because the model cannot see your code; it only sees text. To let the model use external capabilities, you must describe those capabilities in a form it can reason about and emit calls against. The schema provides both the semantics (what the tool does, via the description) and the syntax (the exact argument structure, via the parameter types), so the model can select appropriately and produce a call your code can execute.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You pass the list of tool schemas alongside the messages. The model, at generation time, can produce a structured tool call naming a tool and providing arguments that match its parameter schema, typically enforced by constrained decoding so the arguments are valid. Your agent loop parses that call, runs the corresponding function, and returns the result as a tool-role message. The description and parameter details heavily influence whether the model picks the right tool and fills arguments correctly.

whyImportant: Tool schemas are the interface through which an agent gains real-world capabilities, so writing good ones is a core skill. Vague descriptions or loose types cause the model to call the wrong tool or supply bad arguments, which are among the most common agent failures. Interviewers ask this to see whether you treat tool design as an API design problem with the model as the caller.
realWorldExample: An agent that can search a knowledge base and send email needs two schemas. If the search tool's description is vague, like 'search', the model may call it for tasks it can't handle; a precise description such as 'Search internal documentation for a query and return the top matching passages' steers it correctly. Well-specified required parameters, like a mandatory query string, ensure the model never emits an incomplete call that would fail at runtime.

nestedTopics.title: Name and description
nestedTopics.explanation: The tool name and its description are the model's primary signals for deciding when to use it. The description should state clearly what the tool does, when to use it, and any limits, because the model relies on this natural-language contract rather than any hidden knowledge of your implementation.

nestedTopics.title: Parameter typing and required fields
nestedTopics.explanation: Parameters are specified with types, descriptions, and which are required, often as JSON Schema. Precise types, enums for fixed choices, and clear required flags help the model produce valid, complete arguments and let your code validate them, reducing runtime failures from malformed calls.

nestedTopics.title: The schema as a contract
nestedTopics.explanation: The schema is the shared agreement between the model and your code: the model promises to emit calls matching it, and your code promises to handle any conforming call. Treating it like a public API, with careful naming and documentation, is what makes tool use reliable.

followUps.question: How does the quality of a tool description affect the model's behavior?
followUps.answer: Enormously, because the description is the main thing the model uses to decide whether and how to call the tool. A clear description that states what the tool does, when it is appropriate, what it returns, and any constraints leads the model to select it in the right situations and avoid it otherwise. A vague or overlapping description causes classic failures: the model calls the wrong tool, calls a tool for something it cannot do, or hesitates to use it at all. Since the model has no visibility into your implementation, the description effectively is the tool from its perspective, so writing it carefully, almost like documentation for another engineer, is one of the highest-leverage things you can do for agent reliability.

followUps.question: Why specify required parameters and use enums in a schema?
followUps.answer: Marking parameters as required tells the model it must supply them, preventing incomplete calls that would fail when your code tries to use a missing argument. Using enums to constrain a parameter to a fixed set of allowed values stops the model from inventing invalid options, so instead of guessing a status string it must choose from, say, open, closed, or pending. Both are forms of tightening the contract: they narrow the space of calls the model can produce to only those your code can actually handle, which improves reliability and lets you validate arguments confidently. With constrained decoding, these constraints are enforced during generation, further reducing malformed calls.

question: How do you think about token economics and cost when designing an LLM application?
directAnswer: Token economics means treating tokens as the primary cost and latency driver and designing to minimize wasted tokens without hurting quality. Cost per call is roughly input tokens times the input price plus output tokens times the output price, and output tokens are usually more expensive. Key levers include trimming and summarizing history, using retrieval to include only relevant context, choosing the smallest model that meets quality needs, capping output length, and exploiting prompt caching for repeated context. The goal is to spend tokens where they add value and cut them everywhere they do not.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
Token economics is a budgeting discipline. The per-call cost is approximately:
cost = input_tokens * input_price + output_tokens * output_price
Across an application you also multiply by call volume, so a small per-call saving compounds. It covers both money and latency, since more tokens also mean slower responses.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: This discipline exists because LLM costs scale directly with token usage and can grow surprisingly fast in agent systems, where a single user task may trigger many calls, each resending history and tool definitions. Without deliberate management, redundant context and oversized prompts inflate cost and latency. Thinking in token economics keeps applications affordable and responsive at scale.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You measure token usage per call and per task, then attack the biggest contributors. Long conversation history is trimmed or summarized; large documents are chunked and retrieved rather than pasted whole; verbose system prompts are tightened; output is bounded with max-token limits and concise formatting instructions. Model selection routes easy requests to cheaper models and reserves expensive ones for hard cases. Prompt caching reuses the compute for stable prefixes so repeated context is not re-billed at full price.

whyImportant: Cost and latency are what make or break an LLM product in production, and naive designs can be an order of magnitude more expensive than necessary. Demonstrating that you can reason about tokens as a budget shows engineering maturity beyond making the model merely work. Interviewers ask this because controlling spend is a real, everyday concern for anyone shipping agents.
realWorldExample: An agent that resent a 3,000-token system prompt and a growing history on every step was costing far more than expected under load. The team introduced prompt caching for the stable system prompt and tool definitions, summarized old turns, and routed simple classification steps to a cheaper model. Together these cut per-task cost substantially while keeping quality, illustrating how token-level design choices dominate the economics.

nestedTopics.title: Input versus output cost
nestedTopics.explanation: Providers bill input and output tokens separately, and output is often pricier because it is generated sequentially. This means keeping responses concise and bounding output length can save more than trimming input, so you weigh both sides when optimizing a call.

nestedTopics.title: Context management and retrieval
nestedTopics.explanation: Long histories and large documents are the biggest token sinks. Summarizing old turns, trimming to a sliding window, and using retrieval to include only relevant chunks instead of whole documents dramatically reduces input tokens while preserving the information the model actually needs.

nestedTopics.title: Model selection and caching
nestedTopics.explanation: Choosing the smallest model that meets the quality bar, and routing easy sub-tasks to cheaper models, lowers cost. Prompt caching further reduces the price of repeated stable prefixes, such as a fixed system prompt or tool definitions, by reusing prior computation instead of paying full rate each time.

followUps.question: Why do agent workflows often cost more than a single chat completion?
followUps.answer: Because an agent typically makes many model calls to complete one user task, and each call resends a large amount of context. A single tool-using task might involve the model deciding to call a tool, receiving the result, reasoning again, possibly calling more tools, and finally answering, which is several round trips. Every one of those calls includes the system prompt, the tool schemas, and the accumulating conversation and tool outputs, so tokens are billed repeatedly and the history grows with each step. This multiplication of calls times growing context is why agent workflows can cost far more than a one-shot completion, and it is exactly why history trimming, summarization, and prompt caching matter so much in agent design.

followUps.question: What is the trade-off in choosing a smaller, cheaper model?
followUps.answer: A smaller model costs less per token and usually responds faster, but it may be less accurate, follow instructions less reliably, handle complex reasoning worse, and be more prone to malformed tool calls or hallucination. The trade-off is quality and reliability versus cost and latency. A common strategy is tiered routing: use a cheap model for easy, well-scoped sub-tasks like classification or extraction, and reserve a stronger model for hard reasoning or high-stakes steps. You validate that the cheaper model actually meets the quality bar on your real tasks before switching, because a model that produces subtly wrong output can cost more in downstream errors than it saves in tokens.

question: What is prompt caching and when does it help?
directAnswer: Prompt caching is a provider feature that stores the model's internal computation for a stable prefix of your prompt so that subsequent requests reusing that prefix skip recomputing it, lowering cost and latency. It helps most when many calls share a large, unchanging portion, such as a long system prompt, a set of tool definitions, or a big reference document, followed by a small varying part. Cached input tokens are typically billed at a large discount and processed faster. It is especially valuable in agent loops, where the same system prompt and tool schemas are resent on every step.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
Prompt caching reuses computation for a repeated prefix. Conceptually a request is split into a stable prefix and a variable suffix:
[ system prompt + tool defs + big doc ]  <- cacheable prefix
[ latest user message ]                  <- varies per call
On a cache hit the prefix is not reprocessed from scratch.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It exists because processing input tokens is expensive and much of an agent's prompt is identical from call to call. Recomputing the same long system prompt and tool definitions on every step wastes compute and money. Caching lets the provider store the intermediate state for that unchanging prefix and reuse it, directly attacking the redundant-context cost that dominates agent workflows.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You designate or the provider detects a stable prefix. On the first call it is processed normally and its computed representation is cached for a limited time. On later calls that begin with the exact same prefix, the provider serves the cached representation instead of recomputing it, so you pay a reduced rate for those cached tokens and get lower latency. The cache is prefix-based and exact, so even a small change near the start invalidates it; the varying content must come after the stable part.

whyImportant: Prompt caching is one of the highest-leverage cost optimizations for agents because their prompts are so repetitive. Knowing how to structure prompts to maximize cache hits, stable content first, variable content last, can dramatically cut spend and latency. Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand practical, provider-level optimizations that matter at production scale.
realWorldExample: A support agent has a 4,000-token system prompt plus tool schemas that never change across a conversation, followed by the evolving dialogue. By marking the stable portion as cacheable, each subsequent step in the conversation reuses that prefix at a fraction of the cost and returns faster, since only the new user turn and the growing tail need full processing. Over thousands of conversations this yields large savings with no quality change.

nestedTopics.title: Prefix-based reuse
nestedTopics.explanation: Caching keys on an exact prefix match, so the reusable content must appear at the very start of the prompt and be identical across calls. Anything that changes must go after the cached region, because a difference anywhere in the prefix invalidates the cache from that point on.

nestedTopics.title: Structuring prompts for cache hits
nestedTopics.explanation: To benefit, you order the prompt with the most stable, largest content first: system instructions, tool definitions, and fixed reference material, then the variable per-call input last. This layout maximizes the cacheable prefix and the resulting cost and latency savings.

nestedTopics.title: Limits and expiration
nestedTopics.explanation: Cached prefixes are typically retained only for a limited time and may have minimum size thresholds to be worth caching. Because the cache expires and is exact-match, it helps most for bursts of related calls, like an active conversation or agent loop, rather than sporadic, always-changing prompts.

followUps.question: How should you order a prompt to maximize cache hits?
followUps.answer: Put the most stable and largest content at the very beginning and the most variable content at the end. Concretely, that usually means system instructions first, then tool or function definitions, then any large fixed reference material or documents, and finally the changing per-call content such as the latest user message or the growing conversation tail. Because caching matches on an exact prefix, any change near the start breaks the cache for everything after it, so you never want variable data early in the prompt. Structuring prompts this way turns the bulk of an agent's repeated context into a cacheable prefix, which is where the cost and latency savings come from.

followUps.question: Why might prompt caching not help a particular workload?
followUps.answer: Caching only helps when calls share a substantial, identical prefix that is reused within the cache's lifetime. It does little for workloads where every request is different from the start, where the shared portion is small, or where calls are spread far apart in time so the cached prefix expires before reuse. It can also be undermined by putting variable content, like a timestamp or a user-specific line, early in the prompt, which invalidates the prefix. And if the stable portion is below the provider's minimum cacheable size, caching may not apply. So the benefit is concentrated in agent loops and multi-turn conversations with a large fixed system prompt and tool set, not in one-off, always-unique requests.

question: How do you choose the right model for a given agent task?
directAnswer: Model selection balances capability, cost, latency, context window, and features against the demands of the specific task. You start by defining what the task actually requires: how much reasoning, how long the context, whether it needs tool calling or structured output, and how sensitive it is to errors. Then you pick the smallest, cheapest model that reliably meets that bar, often validating with an evaluation on representative examples. Many systems route different sub-tasks to different models, using cheap fast models for simple steps and strong models for hard reasoning, rather than using one model for everything.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs:
Model selection is a matching problem between task requirements and model attributes. The main axes are:
- capability / reasoning quality
- cost per token (input and output)
- latency / speed
- context window size
- feature support (tools, structured output, vision)
You choose the point that satisfies the task at the lowest cost.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: This process exists because models vary widely in price and ability, and using the most powerful model for everything is wasteful, while using a weak model for a hard task fails. Deliberate selection, and often routing, lets you meet quality requirements affordably. It exists because there is rarely one model that is best on every axis simultaneously.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You characterize the task, then shortlist models whose context window and features fit. You evaluate candidates on a representative set of real inputs, measuring accuracy, format compliance, tool-call correctness, latency, and cost. You pick the cheapest model that clears the quality threshold, and for a multi-step agent you may assign a cheap model to routine steps like classification or extraction and reserve a stronger model for planning or complex reasoning, routing dynamically based on the step or difficulty.

whyImportant: The choice of model shapes an agent's quality, cost, and speed simultaneously, so getting it right has outsized impact. Understanding that stronger is not always better, and that routing can beat a single-model approach, marks an engineer who optimizes systems rather than defaulting to the biggest model. Interviewers ask this to gauge practical judgment about trade-offs under real constraints.
realWorldExample: A document-processing pipeline classifies each incoming document, then for a small subset that needs deep analysis, extracts structured details. The team routes the high-volume classification to a fast, inexpensive model that handles it accurately, and sends only the complex extraction step to a stronger model. This tiered routing keeps overall cost and latency low while preserving accuracy where it matters, which a single strong-model design would not achieve as cheaply.

nestedTopics.title: Matching task to capability
nestedTopics.explanation: Simple, well-scoped tasks like classification, short extraction, or routing often run reliably on smaller models, while multi-step reasoning, nuanced writing, or complex tool orchestration may need a stronger one. Matching the model's capability to the task's actual difficulty avoids both overpaying and underperforming.

nestedTopics.title: Non-capability constraints
nestedTopics.explanation: Beyond raw quality, the context window must be large enough for your prompts, and the model must support needed features like tool calling, structured output, or vision. Latency requirements can also rule out slower large models for interactive use, making these hard constraints alongside quality.

nestedTopics.title: Evaluation and routing
nestedTopics.explanation: Rather than choosing by reputation, you evaluate candidate models on representative real tasks to measure accuracy, format compliance, and cost. In multi-step agents you can route different steps to different models, using a cheaper model where it suffices and a stronger one only where needed.

followUps.question: Why is evaluation on real tasks better than picking a model by benchmark scores?
followUps.answer: Because public benchmarks measure general capabilities that may not reflect your specific task, data distribution, prompts, or failure modes. A model that tops a reasoning leaderboard might still be worse than a cheaper one at your particular extraction format or tool-calling pattern, and benchmark contamination or averaging can hide weaknesses that matter to you. Evaluating on a representative set of your own inputs measures exactly what you care about, accuracy on your task, format compliance, tool-call correctness, latency, and cost, so you make the decision on evidence from your workload rather than a proxy. This is why building even a small internal eval set before choosing or switching models is a standard, high-value practice.

followUps.question: What are the risks of always using the most powerful model?
followUps.answer: The main risks are cost and latency: the strongest models are usually the most expensive per token and often slower, so using them for every step, including trivial ones, inflates spend and hurts responsiveness, especially in agent loops that make many calls. It can also be unnecessary, since many sub-tasks are handled perfectly well by cheaper models, meaning you pay a premium for no quality gain. There can even be reliability downsides if a more verbose or elaborate model over-explains where a terse structured answer was wanted. The disciplined approach is to use the smallest model that meets the quality bar for each step, reserving the powerful model for the parts that genuinely need it.
